passage:
Thursday night.
Today the whole class decided that the maths test was unfair and everyone would sign a complaint. I read the paper again in my head at lunch, and I think it was fair. I said so. The room went quiet, and then everybody spoke at once.
Pradeep asked, “Why are you being difficult?” Two girls looked away. I didn’t sign. I felt my face go hot and my hands go cold.
Now I keep asking myself whether I’m the one who’s wrong. Everyone else can’t be wrong, can they? I can’t decide, and the sad part is that I’m not sure I’d say it again tomorrow.
— Vasudha

qa.q: What did the class decide about the maths test?
qa.a: The class decided the maths test was unfair and that everyone would sign a complaint.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when the room went quiet and then everybody spoke at once?
qa.a: Vasudha felt isolated and pressured, with a hot face and cold hands. Doubt about being wrong is strongest when alone against everyone.

qa.q: What could help Vasudha decide whether the test was really unfair?
qa.a: Vasudha could check the test against what was taught, or quietly ask a trusted adult. That tests the view with facts instead of the pressure of the room.

qa.q: How might Pradeep have seen Vasudha's refusal to sign?
qa.a: Pradeep may have felt frustrated because the class wanted to act together, so a single refusal looked like difficulty. Pradeep may not have meant to push anyone out.

grounding: Shows a student who disagrees with the whole class, feeling isolated and unsure whether the view is wrong.

Gopika: So it's settled, annual day song is the film song?
Meera: Obviously 😅
Rahul: Nobody wants that boring classical one lol
Vikas: I think the classical one could work? It's got that big ending.
Rahul: Lol
Meera: Vikas why are you always like this
Vikas: I just think it'd be different.
Meera: Different = bad
Rahul: Let's just vote already
Meera: Film song, done.
Rahul: 😅
(Gopika, privately): I kind of agree with you. But I can't say it there.
Vikas: Thanks. It felt like everyone was laughing.
Gopika: I know. Don't stop thinking it.

qa.q: What did Vikas suggest for the annual day song?
qa.a: Vikas suggested the classical song because it had a big ending.

qa.q: How can you tell that Vikas felt alone in the group chat?
qa.a: The others laughed and mocked while Vikas wrote defensively, and later said it felt like everyone was laughing. The messages show the lone dissenter's isolation.

qa.q: How could Vikas hold on to the view without turning it into a fight?
qa.a: Vikas could share what is liked about the classical song calmly, and ask what would make the film song a good choice. Having Gopika's quiet support also helps.

qa.q: What might Gopika have been feeling when writing the private message?
qa.a: Gopika probably felt torn, agreeing with Vikas but afraid of being laughed at as well. Writing privately rather than in the group suggests that fear.

grounding: Shows a student disagreeing with the whole class group chat, feeling isolated, with one quiet supporter.

passage: In Class 9, a phone went missing from our classroom, and by lunch the whole class had decided it was Imtiaz, the new boy, because he'd stayed in during PT. Bhavna said it first; soon thirty people agreed. I didn't. I'd seen Imtiaz in the library during PT. When I said so, everyone turned to me. 'You're only saying that because you sit with him,' Bhavna said. My face burned. For a moment I actually wondered if I'd imagined the library. Being the only one felt like standing on a thin plank over water. I said it again anyway, and then I told our class teacher. She checked the library register: Imtiaz had signed in. The phone turned up in the sports room. I'm Varun, and I've never forgotten how heavy that one 'no' felt.

qa.q: Where had Varun seen Imtiaz during PT?
qa.a: In the library.

qa.q: How did Varun feel when the whole class turned round?
qa.a: Varun felt isolated and unsure, face burning, even doubting whether the library memory was real.

qa.q: What did Varun do that helped the truth come out?
qa.a: Repeated what Varun had seen and told the class teacher, who checked the library register.

qa.q: How might Imtiaz have felt while the class blamed him?
qa.a: Frightened and alone, as the new boy accused by thirty people.

grounding: A student who disagrees with the whole class feels isolated and doubts themself, yet the lone view proves right.

passage: Class 11 teacher's note, Tuesday. In today's debate on whether the school should ban phones completely, the whole class voted yes except Kavitha. When she began to explain that some students need phones to reach working parents after school, Bhupen said, 'Nobody agrees with you, Kavitha,' and others laughed. She went quiet and looked down, and I saw her rub her eyes. Afterwards she told me she wondered if she was just being difficult. I told her that standing alone doesn't make an argument wrong, and that her point about working parents was one no one else had considered. Tomorrow I will ask the class to list the best argument from the other side before voting again. I will also speak to Bhupen about his comment.

qa.q: What was Kavitha's reason against a complete phone ban?
qa.a: Some students need phones to reach working parents after school.

qa.q: How was Kavitha feeling after Bhupen's comment?
qa.a: Isolated and unsure, wondering if she was just being difficult, and close to tears.

qa.q: What is the teacher planning, and why might it help?
qa.a: Asking the class to list the best argument from the other side before voting again, and speaking to Bhupen, so dissent is heard rather than laughed off.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see his comment?
qa.a: He may see it as a simple fact or a joke, not realising how alone it made Kavitha feel.

grounding: A teacher's note on a student who stands alone against the class, feels isolated and doubts herself.

passage:
Diary, Thursday night.
The whole group wants to hide Rafiq sir's attendance register tomorrow as a 'joke', because he gave us extra homework. Seven of them said yes in the chat. I wrote, 'Guys, that's not funny, he'll get in trouble with the principal.' Nobody replied for ten minutes. Then Sahil wrote, 'Pranav's scared lol.' Everyone sent laughing faces.
I felt sick. Am I the only one who thinks it's mean? Or am I just boring? Seven against one. Maybe I'm wrong.
But Rafiq sir stayed after class with me twice when I didn't understand trigonometry.
I'm not doing it. I just wish one person had agreed.
Pranav

qa.q: Why did the group want to hide the register?
qa.a: Because Rafiq sir gave them extra homework.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel when everyone sent laughing faces?
qa.a: Sick, isolated and unsure, wondering whether Pranav was wrong or just boring, seven against one.

qa.q: What could help Pranav stay steady?
qa.a: Remembering Rafiq sir's help, and quietly checking whether anyone else in the group privately agrees.

qa.q: How might Rafiq sir be affected if the register disappeared?
qa.a: He could get into trouble with the principal for something he didn't do.

grounding: A student who disagrees with the whole friend group feels isolated and doubts themself, just when the pressure is strongest.
